utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. We have a delayed start because of some technical problems. I'm afraid they are not resolved. In e-court, we don't have the transcript at the moment, only LiveNote. I hope that some technicians will be able to help us. I would like to ask the parties if you have the same problem. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I had a problem until a moment ago with the LiveNote. But as far as I can see, everything is working now, at least on my computer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And how is the situation with the Prosecution, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you. Our system is working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Also the transcript in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Not for the Judges. We should, nevertheless, continue. Before the witness is being brought in, I would like to raise two matters. One has to do with planning of our hearings for the next couple of weeks. Yesterday, the Chamber decided to extend the summer recess for an additional week for an uninterrupted preparation of a possible 98 bis submission by the Defence and to enable members of the teams of the parties of the Prosecution and the Defence to have a longer period for holidays, especially for those, including the members of the team of the Chamber, who want to travel to destinations far away from The Hague. In that case, we will commence in the week of 22nd of August this year, after the summer recess. The remainder of the Prosecution case will then approximately last for two more weeks, hopefully not too much more time, immediately followed by a possible 98 bis submission by the Defence, a response by the Prosecution, and a decision by the Chamber. Is the Defence in a position to indicate if there will be a 98 bis submission? And if so, when will the Defence be in a position to indicate how much time you need, after a possible 98 bis decision by the Chamber, for the preparation of a possible Defence case? Is the Defence in a position to give us some information? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm afraid the Defence is unable at this time to provide this information, but we will do our best to do our planning as soon as possible and provide it to the Court. Of course, one of the reasons why we cannot provide it at this moment is that we are facing a very demanding witness very soon, Expert Witness Richard Butler for the Prosecution, and after his testimony we will have a clearer idea of what to do next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I take it there is some hope that before the summer recess, we would get some more information by the Defence. I think for the moment, this is all we can say about the future schedule. I'm just checking if the transcript is working. Yes, it's working now. Now the transcript in e-court is working also on the screens of the Judges. The witness should be brought in, please. Mr. Vanderpuye, I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to advise the Chamber that P2461 - this is the document that didn't have a translation up-loaded in e-court yet - the translation has been up-loaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document will now be in evidence. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Janc. Our apologies for the delay. We had some technical problems before we could really start the proceedings. May I remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies. Yesterday, the Prosecution tendered three -- no, six intercepts, six documents. The Chamber has considered this application. The Chamber notes that the Defence has no objection to their admission, and, therefore, the Chamber decided to receive these six documents into evidence. Mr. Registrar, could you provide us with the numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 5568 shall be assigned Exhibit P2463. 65 ter document 5570 shall be assigned Exhibit P2464. 65 ter document 5573 shall be assigned Exhibit P2465. 65 ter document 5579 shall be assigned Exhibit P2466. 65 ter document 5580 shall be assigned Exhibit P2467. And, finally, 65 ter document 5582 shall be assigned Exhibit P2468. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, you may now continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to greet everyone present. I wish peace unto this house, and may this day in court and the final judgement reflect God's will. May there be -- may the proceedings end in keeping with God's will, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will pick up where we left off yesterday concerning what Chief of Staff General Rose said concerning the allegations of the American service and the information that leaked from American sources to the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir's microphone be brought closer to him, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you have information that representatives of the UNPROFOR shared information with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we call up in e-court D189, marked for identification. Thank you very much. Could we rotate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a dispatch from the State Security Sector in Gorazde, dated 18 June. It reads: "The MUP of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the State Security chief." Then: "Reference." And the text goes: "Concerning your request in the above telegram, we hereby advise you that we conducted an interview with Colonel Roger from the BritBat." And: "In this interview Roger confirmed the information we had received from Officer Allen and said that regrouping of aggressor forces, two to three brigades strong, had been observed in the area of Trnovo. He also said this should not concern us because, according to his assessment, there were about 1500 to 1600 aggressor soldiers?" Signed: "Midhat Senovic, chief of the State Security Sector." Now, is it evident from this dispatch that BritBat intelligence officers were sharing information with the BH Army, thus taking sides in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from this document we can see that they were in contact with the BiH side and that they shared certain information with them.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now call up D188, also MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last document we just have seen on the screen was MFI'd. I don't know why it was MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was tendered, but not admitted into evidence yet. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we will tender all this after Mr. Tolimir finishes his questioning, and then we would deal with this issue, with your leave. Translations were missing, and there were some other problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The other problems, I was told by the Registry, were that there was no witness yet to identify and authenticate the previous document. We will see whether you will tender this document again. Go ahead, please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would now like to call up D188, also MFI'd. Thank you. Now we have it on the screen. It's poorly legible. It's another date from the State Security Service Sector in Gorazde, dated 2nd of July, 1995. I'll quote from the first page. This is sent to an assistant minister and head of the State Security Service in Bosnia-Herzegovina: "We hereby inform you that on 1st July 1995, Colonel John Riley, UNPROFOR commander in Gorazde, invited us to a short informal visit, indicating that he was happy to share with us some information he had obtained in a telephone conversation with General Smith."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: After this first quotation, can we see that this officer was collecting certain intelligence while being UNPROFOR commander in Gorazde in a certain way, and that he is making promises to share that information which he had obtained from General Smith?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I quote from the second paragraph: "On this occasion, Colonel John told us that Karadzic's terrorists, with a view to relieving their forces around Sarajevo, planned to launch an attack in the area of Sapna and Kalesija in the next few days (he didn't know exactly when)." It goes on to say: "Further in the conversation, Colonel John indicated the possibility that in the coming period, following extensive mobilisation, Karadzic's terrorists were planning ..." And then I can't read the text that follows. But then it says: "... attack enclaves in Eastern Bosnia. According to General Smith, there are two alternatives, two variants of the Chetnik plans, the first to carry out an attack and take control of Srebrenica and Zepa, which according to the Chetniks is an easier task, and the other being to attack and take control of Gorazde, which is a more difficult task, bearing in mind the fact that the Chetniks engaged about 10.000 troops in the attack on Gorazde in April 1994 without being able to enter the town." "We note that in a similar situation in May 1995, Colonel John Riley informed us that on a specific day, Tuzla would be shelled, which proved perfectly correct, and we duly informed you about it." My question is: Can we see from this report that the UNPROFOR commander in Gorazde is sharing intelligence and information he obtained through his command concerning the strength of the forces of Republika Srpska, forces to which they refer as the aggressor?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would have another question. Did you notice in the last paragraph, it's a reference to a shelling of Tuzla that is yet to happen? Is it possible to know something that hasn't happened yet unless you are, yourself, involved in that operation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that you have intelligence on what is planned. On -- for example, here we have information that Tuzla will be shelled in the future, and this might be coming out of some intelligence. And this incident then, indeed, took place, so it means that the intelligence was precise. It doesn't necessarily mean that you should be involved in this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then doubt the authenticity of this document, since you've just said that there was information that turned out to be accurate?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several ways how to prove the authenticity of any document, and also, in this regard, one of the ways is also checking what is written there and how accurate that is. And I can say, for this document, that it looks authentic to me, yes, although it would be always better to talk and -- to the source of this document first to confirm exactly how it was produced, when, and by whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We would like to do that, too, but the Prosecution did not bring such witnesses, and we cannot call them because they don't want to come when invited by us. Judge Mindua asked yesterday, after you said you doubt the veracity of certain information provided by the Army of Republika Srpska, he asked for what reason, and you said that you were drawn to that conclusion by the fact that I said that information was sometimes deliberately distorted and there was a lot of deliberate misinformation. I would like to ask you: Is it quite normal and usual to try to deceive and dis-inform the enemy in the course of an air battle?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it's normal. But based on my expertise, which is a little bit different than yours, I can't say and confirm how often would that happen. So but from what I know and what I gained throughout the investigation here, I know that such issues occurred as well, so -- but I can't be more precise than that because I'm not a big expert in intelligence -- intelligence services.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But please tell us -- the information we read yesterday when you said that, that was information from the Main Staff, sent exclusively to the Army of Republika Srpska. The person who processed the information, are they allowed to send misinformation to their own troops or are they allowed to send misinformation only to enemy troops? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, generally speaking, it's always better that you have or you provide the accurate information to your own troops, unless you want to do something which you don't want your troops would know in advance. So everything is possible, but in generally speaking, yes, most information, I assume, are correct which are provided to your troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I just would like to make one remark. You said: "... we cannot call these witnesses because they don't want to come when invited by us." I think you are well informed about your rights in preparation of the Defence case. There may be some reluctance by certain persons you want to have in court, but you know if you call them, if you would include them in your 65 ter witness list, there are measures to be taken by the Court to bring them to The Hague and to testify here pursuant to our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. So it's up to you to decide if you want to call them. I just want to make this very clear on the record. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for these instructions and guide-lines. Could we now have D248 on e-court. And before that, I tender the two documents we used. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, can you help me? Have you ever seen this document which is on the screen now and the previous one you were asked about the content?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's quite possible I've seen them before, because they are part of the OTP collection, but I can't confirm for the fact right now that these are the two that I reviewed during the my work for the OTP here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Have you any information how this document and the previous one came into the possession of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, right now I can't say anything about how the OTP came into possession of these documents. For that, I would need to take a look into the electronic database to see how did we receive them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Colonel John Riley?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was commander of the UNPROFOR troops in Gorazde at the time. But, again, I would need to check and confirm that, checking the records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye, I saw you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think you quite covered some of my concerns, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What are your concerns? What is your position in relation to the tendering of these two documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We don't have an objection to it, in light of -- in light of the questioning that's been conducted by the Court concerning Mr. Janc' familiarity with at least some of the content of the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Both documents will now be received into evidence, D188 and D189.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these documents have been admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I asked for D248, point 209 of that document. Thank you. 61 in English and 77 in Serbian. Thank you. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The security of the armed forces in the course of the war." In item 209, we have a definition of the degree of veracity of intelligence which may be accurate, probable, dubious or false. And then it says: "Accurate intelligence is intelligence whose credibility is corroborated with evidence. In most cases, it is confirmed by several sources or obtained from the gathering organs or a single reliable source, or from gathering organs several times." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As you answered this question more or less in the same way as described in this book, just tell us whether you and I have given a proper definition and always spoken of the veracity of documents in line with the fact that they have to be corroborated in practice.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, I can agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, there was mention here of a letter to van Baal, sent by General Milovanovic. That was 65 ter, I think, 774, but I'm not sure. My legal adviser will check this. Please, while we are waiting for the document to come up: You will recall that there was a dispute there because van Baal was detained at a check-point, and he complained to General Milovanovic. My question is as follows: Are you aware, as you have read the agreement on control of movement on the territory of Republika Srpska, on the basis of the documents you have studied, was personal property subject to inspection and control? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure now. I would need to check or to see the actual agreement again to find this provision there, if it is there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It's P2443. Can it be brought up in e-court. Thank you. Yesterday, it was shown as 7445. Perhaps there is a translation. Now we see there's no translation. It's an UNPROFOR document written on the 18th of July, 1994, where General van Baal says that on the 15th of July, he was detained at the check-point. They wanted to look at his personal things, and he refused. And he wrote about this, complaining to General Milovanovic. Based on this, Milovanovic sent him a letter apologising for the inconvenience he had undergone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Based on these documents, can you answer my question or do we need to look at the agreement on movement, 977 -- or, rather, D77? Could we look at D77 to make it easier for the witness to answer the question. Thank you. Thank you. We see only the English version now. Ah, here is the Serbian version. This document was drawn up in the Main Staff of the Sarajevo Forward Command on the principles of freedom of movement. Please glance through it so you can answer the questions. And can you see that it says that personal property will not be checked? After you've read page 1, please ask to be shown page 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, before I start reading this, I would like to point out this document is dated 31st of January, 1995, so it's most probably agreement which entered into force after that date. And this incident with General van Baal happened in July 1994, so we don't know what kind of agreement was in force at that time. So I can read this and confirm what's written here, but it still doesn't answer the question if this was, indeed, the case, the same regulations were in place at the time of the incident.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If you have read this, could we turn to page 2. Could e-court show page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is as follows: Is there anything in this agreement about personal property of those passing through check-points not being checked? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on the first page, there is a provision that goods which are in vehicles together with the convoy should be checked, and if anything which is not on the list approved beforehand is found can be confiscated. That, I think, is a provision there. So it's not that precise regarding personal belongings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware of any agreement, signed on the territory of the former SFRY during the war, where an exception was made for personal belongings when dealing with check-points and the control of goods and people passing through check-points?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any agreement in mind right now, but I do remember, for example, convoy notifications and approvals from the VRS side allowing, for example, the UNPROFOR staff to carry their own weapons, for example, through check-points, something like that. I do remember such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is: Were personal weapons visible, were they easy to see, and therefore they could be checked visually? You would know this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most -- in most occasions, yes, I would say you would see these personal weapons which is carried by -- by the soldiers. They would be visible, yes, but sometimes not, because you can carry it under cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it say here that goods not reported beforehand can be confiscated, and would concealed weapons be included?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say what "goods" would entail. I would say for sure what was part of the transport. What was carrying through the check-point, if that entail also the confiscated weapons, I'm not sure, based on this document only.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware whether members of UNPROFOR could carry three or four or five rifles into an area and then come back with only one?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how much -- actually, how many rifles they could carry, so I think that was part of agreement -- part of an agreement between UNPROFOR and your side, so for them, to how many rifles they can carry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As in this case we were not dealing with weapons, but personal documents, I have no further questions on this. Yesterday, you were shown 65 ter 05598. I didn't manage to note down the number under which it was admitted. It's 65 ter 05598.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 5598 has been admitted into evidence under Exhibit P2460. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please repeat. Your microphone was not switched on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I asked for document P2460 to be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see this document. Yesterday, your attention was drawn by the Prosecutor to line 17, where it says that there was a farewell ceremony in Banja Luka for 17 retiring generals of the VRS. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Along with this document, there is also P4621 [as interpreted]. Could we have P4621, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, as it was admitted into evidence yesterday? It's P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is P2461.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P2461.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, is the title "Relieved of the Hitherto Duty and Placed at the Disposal of the Yugoslav Army": "Tolimir (son of Stanko) Zdravko ... born on the 27th of November, 1948"? So is he being pensioned off or is he being placed at the disposal of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would be better to say that he was placed at the disposal of the Yugoslav Army, and at the same time you were relieved of duty from the VRS army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have 05525 on the 65 ter list of the Prosecutor. I didn't note down the number under which it was admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is Exhibit P2437. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Based on this document, you confirmed that I was a major general as of the year 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May it be admitted into evidence? Thank you. Could we now have 1D00196 [as interpreted]. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, these documents are already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, I just want the witness to see them. 1D00916. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now you have given two different numbers. Could you please correct -- tell us which is the correct one? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last number on the transcript, 1D916.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Have you found, among the documents, this decree of the president of Republika Srpska terminating service in the Army of Republika Srpska in order to retire and move to the reserve force a certain number of troops and officers? One of them is General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I've seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a document dated 17 October 1997 -- sorry, 1995. My question is: Can we see, from the title of the document, that a general can also be transferred from active service to the reserve force?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that -- that's what it says here, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D916 shall be assigned Exhibit D298. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You were shown yesterday 65 ter 05549 that received Exhibit P2455. May I call it up now in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is behind tab 7 of the binder we received yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see this document on the screen. It says that on the 30th June, General Tolimir is standing in for General Mladic and is approving a certain request.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Did you have any other documents to make the claim that General Tolimir was standing in for General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from a document which was also drafted by the authorities of the Republic of Croatia, that intelligence report, we have no other documents related to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In this document that is before us, a document that you used and the Prosecutor tried to use as a basis to prove that I was standing in for General Mladic, is there any solid information about that or is it just a comment by the intercept operator?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this intercept, which is a summary, actually, of the actual conversation, we only see in brackets -- I can say the comment of the intercept operator, that General Tolimir is "standing in for General Mladic." But we cannot conclude from that, what is in brackets, if that was actually said during the conversation or how that intercept operator concluded that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have, among your documents, reports from the Main Staff dated 30th June or the next date, 31st of June, and could you see on these documents who signed combat reports and other documents? Do you have ERN numbers for these combat reports?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure we have a lot of documents from around these dates and also, I'm sure, some from that date, and, yeah, I would need to take a look into the documents, who signed them. And I think I've checked for your name and I couldn't see your name as a signatory on that date, except, I think, on that intelligence report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we will not waste time looking for those ERN numbers. If you had found them, you would have certainly provided them. Let me ask you: If I was standing in for General Mladic, would it have been logical for me to sign documents on his behalf as well, and have you found such signatures anywhere?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be logical you would sign these documents for him if you are standing in, but the problem here is that we certainly don't have the entire collection, all documents which you produced on these dates in our collection. So we have a lot of documents which are missing from your collection, so we don't know, actually, what was signed on that date. The second problem is that we don't need -- that we don't know, from this intercept, for how long you have been standing in. Was that for one day, several hours on that day, or a few consecutive days? So these are the problems. And if General Mladic was missing for only a few hours or one day, it's not necessary you would find any document, because perhaps no documents were provided on that day that would need any signature. So it's just my speculation, but we don't have any such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When the commander is not in the area of responsibility, in this case Republika Srpska, whereas his chief of staff is present, do you know that nobody else is allowed to stand in for the commander but the chief of staff? Do you know that rule?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I know that rule, yes, and I'm sure that the witness following me will be in a much better position to explain this, better than me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We'll ask the witness who comes after you, but just tell me your opinion about this. P244 is the next document I would like to call up in e-court, Article 10. It's the wrong number. Sorry. While my adviser finds the right number, let us look at 65 ter 05827, a document you used to try to prove what was contained in the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember that? That's a report from the Intelligence Administration of the Croatian Army from 31st July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now P2459. No, sorry, P2458.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just look now at P2458.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is this a report from the Intelligence Administration of the Army of Croatia, dated 30th July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us look at paragraph 1. It reads: "After the successful attack by the Croatian Army and the Croatian Defence Council on the Grahovo-Glamoc front-line, and the creation of prerequisites for directly threatening Knin, the local Serb population is still obviously in fear and panic, which are intensified by the news of the HV grouping forces and preparing to attack the entire RSK territory." According to this intelligence, did the Croatian Army attack Republika Srpska and Republic of Serbian Krajina before the 30th July, as this report says?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it's possible that it was also before, but not necessarily. It might be also on that day, on 30 of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, this report from the Intelligence Administration is dated "Zagreb, 31st of July 1995," and it's called an intelligence report for the 30th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is the 31st of July, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us look now at page 2, because it's important, since you said that General Tolimir was sent to Glamoc and Grahovo because they had been captured. We can now see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the English, it should be page 3, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It's page 3. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us look at this section headed "Bosanska Grahovo and Glamoc area." Let us look at the fifth paragraph below the heading. It says: "During the day, General Tolimir (chief of security) and General Djukic (assistant commander for logistics) from the VRS Main Staff have been sent to the Grahovo-Glamoc front-line in order to consolidate the situation and undertake measures to consolidate the forces. For this purpose, a special team will be set up on the -- in the assembly area of the 2nd Krajina Corps in Drvar, in keeping with the directive of Mr. Karadzic." It says --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters be given the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "In addition to staffing reinforcements in the command of the SVK and VRS commands, these commands carried out activities to prepare and bring in reinforcement to ensure conditions for launching a counter-attack on HV forces ..." Et cetera. Can we see from this that Tolimir was, indeed, sent to the area of Grahovo and Glamoc?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's written there that you were sent along with General Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it an unlawful activity to send two generals into their native places in order to organise forces for defence against the Croatian aggression that had been launched at the time against Grahovo and Glamoc? Would that be illegal, wrong?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is nothing wrong with it. I think it is legitimate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at the next page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us look at the next page, because this document no longer refers to the units of the Army of Republika Srpska. It deals, down below, with units of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page do you want to have on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone, please, microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last page. The last page, to see who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's the penultimate page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was this signed by the chief of the Intelligence Service of the Croatian Army, Rear Admiral Davor Domazet, also known as Loso?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the document, we can see a typed signature of this individual, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see on this page that the document was sent to a number of addresses, officials and leaders of the Croatian Army and the defence ministry?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you, in examination-in-chief, whether authenticity is also confirmed that it was sent -- by the fact that it was sent to a number of persons. My question is: Can the veracity of anything be judged on the basis of the number of addressees or does it have to be confirmed by double-checking and further corroborating information?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is always better to be confirmed by double-checking and further corroborating.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now look at a report dated 30th July that you also used -- or the 31st July that was also used by the Prosecution to prove authenticity. 65 ter 7450, that's the number I noted down. I'm not sure if it's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now P2456.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is a report from 1 July 1995. We can see the Croatian word for "July" here. Let us see the second page now, where it says "Bosnian Grahovo and Glamoc area." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The subheading is "Other Activities." It says: "After our meeting with the commander of the UN forces for ex-Yugoslavia, General Brinkman, on 29 June in Zvornik, General Mladic left for Belgrade and, during that day, spent time at the Main Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. During his stay in Belgrade, he is also scheduled for a medical check-up at the Military Medical Academy because of Mladic's kidney problems. In his absence, General Mladic will be replaced by the chief of staff -- by the chief of security of the Main Staff of the VRS, General Tolimir." Those people who are making this claim, do they have any grounds for it or are they just blindly accepting the comment made by the intercept operator? Have you seen any primary-source document on this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From information we can see on the screen now, we can't say what was the source for the Government of Croatia to put this information into this intelligence report, so we can't say was that, for example, an intercept or any other independent intelligence, other information they obtained through other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, does one appoint a replacement if one is just going for a medical check-up? Is it something that takes a long time or is it just a very brief absence, perhaps shorter than the meeting General Mladic had in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for how long this medical check would be needed, so it might be several hours or even shorter or longer period.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't receive any interpretation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's apology. We did not turn on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please repeat, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asking: Has the witness found any documents, in his capacity as investigator, from which we could see what General Mladic was doing the next day? Did he have any communication with the commanders, and UNPROFOR, and other forces in his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would need to double-check that. I'm sure I've seen some reports or some information that he is back at the beginning of July already. But for exact dates and exact information, I would need to take a look into further documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have you perhaps seen a document saying that General Mladic returned the very next day and pursued his regular activities after that medical check-up at the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that document right now, but if you have it available, I would like to see it and I can comment it on if I came across this document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just briefly, I noted that at page -- at the end of page 27, line 25, into page 28, line 2, the witness stated that he had some information that General Mladic was back at the beginning of July already. And in the context of this line of questioning, we're talking already about the end of July, so I just wanted to clarify that. My inclination is that the witness was -- meant to say the end of August, but maybe he can clarify that just so the record is clear. Or, rather, the beginning of August, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, could you clarify that? To which date or time-period were you referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was correct, actually. I was referring to July, and I still think that you're talking about July, because the document in front of us is dated 29 of June, when he's going to Belgrade. So he's back in Bosnia at the beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, are you able to finish your cross-examination before the break? We started a bit later, so that we are now -- we should have the break five minutes before 4.00. I just want to inquire your position. How much additional time do you need?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's better to go on the break, and then after the break I have perhaps just two or three more questions, if you allow me. But if you don't allow it, I can finish now, since the witness has answered this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There's no need to stop you in your cross-examination. I just wanted to inquire if it's better to have the break now or if you're able to finish. We will take our break now, and we will resume 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like e-court to show P2458, document P2458. Thank you. Please, for the sake of the record, let us say that this is information dated the 31st of July, as it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So that's July; is that right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for this document, it's dated 31st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we look at page 2 now. Thank you. It's page 3 in English. In the third paragraph, can we also see that it says, the 30th of July: "The communications system between Knin and Drvar which previously also included Grahovo and Glamoc, attempts are being made to redirect it, and this system must be ready to work by 2400 hours on 30th of July"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have the next page. Thank you. So let's look at page 4 in the Serbian language and page 8 in English so as to avoid discussing areas not covered by the examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at the chapter dealing with the 7th Knin Corps. It says here, in the last paragraph: "With regard to providing security during the visit by General Mladic and Patriarch Pavle, a police unit (company) from Knin has not been sent to the Dinara area (Jancija Glava - elevation 1525), and it is estimated that it will be sent to the said area after the above-mentioned officials arrive." My question is as follows: Is it evident from this that General Mladic visited Knin immediately after being in Belgrade, according to what it says here?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what it says in this document, which is from 31st of July, 1995, we can see that and conclude that General Mladic was in Knin area. But what we cannot say from this document is that he was in Belgrade before -- just before that. He was in Belgrade at the end of June 1995, based on the previous document, so it's one month of difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, all right. And can you see what it says here, "The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska"? It's the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it say that on the 31st of July, a meeting would be held in Mrkonjic Grad between General Mladic and General Smith? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go back to page 2 now. Thank you. It's page 3 in English. Thank you. In the third -- or, rather, fourth paragraph, it says: "During the day, General Tolimir (chief of security) and General Djukic (assistant commander for logistics) from the Main Staff have been sent to the Grahovo-Glamoc front-line in order to consolidate the situation and undertake measures to consolidate the forces." So that's the 2nd Corps in Drvar. Does it transpire from this that General Tolimir and General Mladic were on the territory of the Drvar Corps together on those dates, the dates mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say from the document that they were down there together, but they were both at that area at around same time, end of July, on 30 July and 31st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 296, D -- 2D26 [as interpreted], page 16 in Serbian and English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We didn't receive the English translation of the number. Please repeat. Mr. Gajic, you may help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D296.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As we can see, it is the interview you had with Mile Micic, and it says here: "I am Dusan Janc," where you are introducing yourself. And you mentioned this yesterday in the course of your examination. Thank you. So now look at page 16, please. Thank you. We can see the first page here -- or, rather, page 16 - thank you - the first paragraph, where it says Mile Micic, whom you interviewed, was asked how long the operation lasted, and he says: "... I don't know exactly, but maybe around seven to ten days." So he's speculating, he's speculating about the time-period. "... until the moment when Grahovo and Glamoc fell, and I think that was at the end of July or the very beginning of August. Then, from Boksanica or from the surroundings of Zepa, we went to Banja Luka or Drvar." Do you recall that Mile Micic said this to you when you were interviewing him in the OTP premises in Sarajevo in 2009? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that, and I can confirm that he said that during the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told that perhaps some translation issue was on the first page. As you are just dealing with dates of this interview in 2009, you should have a look on pages 1 in both versions and to check if there's anything wrong with it. If you look at the headline, it is said "Interview with Mile Micic Conducted in the OSCE Offices in Banja Luka on the 24th of August, 2009." In the B/C/S, it is the 17th of November, 2009. There seems to be a certain inconsistency. First, Mr. Gajic - he was the first on his feet - and then Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we noticed the discrepancy. Mr. Elderkin from the OTP told me a few days ago that this is a mistranslation. Perhaps the witness could clarify on what date this interview was held, whether it was the 17th of November or the 24th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That is my understanding as well. I had a chance to speak to Mr. Elderkin a few days ago, but I think the date, as you can see in the text of the interviews, themselves, is translated -- is properly reflected in the content of the interview, rather than in the headings respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, we see at the beginning "EG," it seems to be Erin Gallagher - is referring to November the 17th at 3.10 in the afternoon. Mr. Janc, do you recall when this interview was conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. From -- it was on 17 November 2009, and it was conducted at the Sarajevo Field Office, not in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The field office is located in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. After this clarification, you may continue, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to thank everyone. Let's go back to page 16 now, which we were looking at before this intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You go on to ask Mile Micic: "Just the two of you?" He says: "We went to Banja Luka or Drvar." He says: "Just the two of you?" He says: "Yes." You say: "And how long did you stay at that area, then?" "At which area?" he said. And you said: "To Banja Luka and Drvar." And he says: "All the time until the Dayton Peace Agreement was signed, because the general was in -- I don't want to say team, but in that delegation. He left some 10 days before the Dayton Peace Agreement was signed, and I returned from that area sometime around the 1st of December." Please, tell me, do you recall that the witness said this, and can you confirm that this is what he actually told you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that, and I can confirm that's what he told us. And everything can be double-checked because this interview was tape-recorded, so everything is on a tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We ask you this because this witness left earlier because of some problems. He was not cross-examined, so we didn't get the chance to ask him this, but you have now confirmed it. Thank you for all the replies you have given to the questions put to you. The Defence thanks you. God bless you, and good fortune in your future work. Thank you. Mr. President, the Defence has finished its cross-examination of this witness. I wish to thank everyone who participated in this testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Just one clarification. You said that you didn't get the chance to ask him this. You know it was your decision not to cross-examine the witness. So you had the chance, but you didn't use the chance, just for the sake of the record. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, you may recall -- I don't have the transcript reference here handy, but I think we all recall that you were asked some questions concerning General Tolimir, in respect of an intercept, asking you some things about standing in for General Mladic. Do you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the intercept I'm thinking of, which I think was referred to, was the 30 June 1995 intercept. Yes, it's at page 19, line 20 through 23, where you asked -- the exhibit number is P2455, this 30 June intercept. And, in particular, you were asked about the circumstances under which an individual would stand in for the commander. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You replied that it was not clear from the intercept how long or how short a period of time General Tolimir might have been standing in for General Mladic. Do you recall the testimony, perchance, of Ljubomir Obradovic in this case concerning the assignment or appointment of a stand-in in the commander's absence or in the absence of the commander as well as the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can remember him testifying here, but I can't recall this exact portion of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would just refer the Trial Chamber to transcript pages 11936 through 937, and he was asked, in particular in the context of whether he was present at the Main Staff in 1995, whether he was aware of Mladic being absent. And in response, he indicated that: "When the commander goes somewhere, he appoints one of his assistants to stand in for him during his absence." And then he goes on to name the various assistants in the Main Staff Command. And then further on, he says -- and this is at transcript page 12019 to 12020, when he was questioned by the Presiding Judge. He basically said that if the chief of staff is temporarily absent and the commander has to go away, then he will select one of his assistants that's present to stand in for him while he's away. Given Mr. Obradovic's testimony, does that in any way inform your answer with respect to General Tolimir's questions about the propriety of his apparently standing in for General Mladic on the 30th of June, as indicated in the intercept?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this would support the intercept, itself, that he -- it's possible that he has been standing in at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you find anything, when you were looking at this material, that contradicts that intercept, or, actually, any of the intercepts that you looked at?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You were asked a series of questions by General Tolimir, as you may recall, about another intercept. I have the 65 ter number as 5544, but I know it was admitted. It's P2452. This was an intercept which involved the use of a translator, and there was some issue made about a designation in a MUP intercept indicating that it had been translated from English. Do you recall that part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In particular, you were asked a question about a certain Svetlana, and that is, thankfully, pointed out at page 16152, lines 9 through 12, and then you were asked about that on cross-examination as well. I want to show you P698 in relation to your answers concerning the questions put to you by General Tolimir about who Svetlana was, who did she interpret for, whether she interpreted on the UNPROFOR side or on the VRS side. And I believe you answered that you thought that she interpreted for the UNPROFOR side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this was at transcript page 16214, line -- it looks like line 11. And here we were able to identify a few intercepts in evidence in this case - one is P698, another is P702 - and here you can see a reference to Svetlana. This is from 9 July, at 1240 hours, and you can see her directly referenced in this intercept. Is this the same Svetlana that you had in mind in answering those questions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, and I think that I also referred to a conversation between General Nicolai and General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have an audio of this recording. I don't know if you'd be interested in hearing it. But in that audio-recording - and it does involve General Tolimir and General Nicolai, mediated by Svetlana - I think you will be able to hear some English spoken in that intercept, and perhaps that may be helpful to the Trial Chamber, in terms of Mr. Janc' testimony concerning his views on the MUP intercept that was the subject of some discussion. It is in evidence already, so if it's of interest to the Trial Chamber, I'll be happy to play it out. It's about four or five minutes long. But if not, then I'm happy to conclude my redirect examination at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said it is already in evidence. Under this P number, 698, or with a different exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The one that's on the screen at the moment looks like P702, but also there's P698. They're both audio recordings, and I can play either one of them, I think, with the assistance of the Court. But since they're both admitted, it's really -- I'll leave it in your hands, and you can let me know what you prefer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think there's no need to spend five minutes with that. It is in evidence. It can be checked by the parties and, of course, by the Chamber in finding our findings. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That concludes my redirect examination. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Janc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, you will be pleased to hear that this now, hopefully, concludes your testimony here in this trial. If there are not unforeseeable circumstances, this will be your last day in this courtroom with this Chamber. Thank you very much that you were able to provide us with your expertise and knowledge. Now you are free to return to your normal activities. That means to your work here for the OTP. Thank you very much. Have a good day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. McCloskey. Welcome back. Is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours, everyone. Yes -- yes, he is. He's right outside. And if I could just give you a little -- just a bit of a preview of what we were -- had in mind, just from a logistics point of view. Fundamentally, Mr. Butler will be talking about some of the documents and materials and intercepts that were the subject-matter of his reports and his previous testimony and review. And as such, I have three binders of these materials that I will be fundamentally going through with him, and he -- because, as you know, it's easier to deal with hard copies, and that's the way we have done this, as it's happened before. So Mr. Butler will have three binders. I -- yeah, he has one now. Ms. Stewart has the two others that we'll give to him or make available to him, you know, before he starts, because we don't, obviously, want to be giving him things after we start. But hopefully he'll be able to find a place to put them. We have provided both General Tolimir and Mr. Gajic with their own sets of binders with materials, and we have -- and I don't mean this to be -- to look too intimidating over here behind Ms. Stewart. If the Trial Chamber would like also, I mean, this -- he's going to be on for several days, and looking hard in this computer can be difficult. I'm sure they're not going to be perfect, though a lot of hard work has gone into them. You're welcome to have those, but, of course, e-court and the court system is fundamentally what we'll be going from. But we have these binders if -- if -- we also have some for the Court, the Legal Officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I look at these binders, this is really a threat. I don't know where to put them and to handle them. But sometimes it's, indeed, helpful to have hard copies in front of us. Perhaps you can provide us with the first binder, and we can receive the others at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can manage that. So you just leave them on the bench and we'll get them back each day, or if you want to take any of them with you; however -- but we can manage the actual hauling around of it. This is the way we used to do it before e-court, so it's bringing back memories.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We would appreciate getting an additional binder for the staff of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we have that as well, is my understanding. And, Mr. President, many of the documents in the collection are in evidence. Many are not. You have -- obviously will have seen many of these documents, so I will try not to overdo it with matters that you've seen, and you'll, hopefully, notice that. And as we go through that, there are three documents that did not have 65 ter numbers that I've alerted Mr. Gajic to, and that we'll talk about that and see if there's any problem there. All the rest are on the 65 ter list. There's a fourth, but that was Mr. Butler's revised CV that we revised upon him getting here and putting in his latest, so I'm sure there won't be any objection to that fourth document. And, lastly, as I have before, I -- and I know you will, I encourage you to -- please don't -- please interrupt me at any point and -- because I'm, of course, trying to present the material that will help you answer the questions you need to answer. But no problem with interruptions, and I think that would be, overall, helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Butler. Welcome to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. Just for the record, you have a binder in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You received this binder from the Prosecution, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And it is, up to now, only one binder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up to now, it's labelled "Binder 1 of 3," so I expect there will be two more somewhere in the process, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Unfortunately for you. Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you state your name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My name is Richard Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us, what is your current work and profession?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I am an intelligence officer. I am currently employed by the US Department of Homeland Security, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement, where I work as the intelligence operations manager for the Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I am going to remind myself and you that we need to go a little bit slower than we, frankly, have done before, because, as you know, General Tolimir is representing himself and is an active participant, unlike the other cases, where there has been an attorney that spoke English. So I will try to delay, and we will both try to do that. And if we could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And especially you should both pause between question and answer. That's the most important thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to 65 ter 7436.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a new 65 ter number, but it's your updated resume that you did for us recently. I won't go through it completely. I see that you've done a summary of your professional background as a professional intelligence officer, and we'll get to that. But you've just told us what your current job is for the United States. Can you tell us how long you have had that -- you worked for that organisation, and just, basically, what your job has been.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I began with Immigration and Customs Enforcement in February of 2004, and shortly thereafter I started working human rights violator cases, as they're known in our law enforcement vernacular. I've been doing that more or less full time now since about 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your job before that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Before that, not only did I do human rights violator cases, but I would also work more traditional law enforcement issues; for example, human smuggling and trafficking, other such crimes. But because of my unique background, in part from my time here at the ICTY, and my military intelligence background, clearly my current employers believed I was more suited to be doing war crimes full time than other forms of criminal activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who did you -- what organisation did you work for before the United States Government?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Before the United States Government employed me, I was an analyst for the ICTY Office of the Prosecutor for a total of almost seven years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we'll get into that in more detail, but can you tell us -- you used the vernacular "human rights violator" cases that you're involved in. Can you tell us what that involves and your role in it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That phrase is how we define investigations that are conducted by our agency relating to individuals who have committed human rights violations or war crimes in other countries prior to coming to the United States, where they have gained some form of immigration benefit. And in conducting -- in committing those crimes, they're not eligible for those benefits under our law, so it is, in part, the job of our agency to investigate those allegations. And when we can confirm those allegations, we bring either criminal or administrative proceedings against the accused in order to strip him or her of the immigration benefits that were derived by misrepresenting facts related to their involvement in those kinds of crimes. It could be as simple as, you know, individual acts of persecution. In some cases, it could be denying their involvement in acts of genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your work now, several years for the United States that you've just described, were you involved in the investigation and prosecution of anyone that had been involved in war crimes in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you give us any -- a brief example of one -- one case that was -- that you were involved in and that was prosecuted by the United States?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Perhaps one of the better examples is the case of an individual named Marko Boskic, who, in July of 1995, was a member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment and was one of the individuals who directly participated in the executions at Branjevo Farm. Following his involvement in those crimes by a number of years, he made his way to the United States and ultimately became a lawful permanent resident. As a result of investigation that was undertaken by our agency and other law enforcement agencies, we were able to criminally prosecute him for the crimes related to his lying on immigration applications to gain that legal permanent resident status. He was convicted of those crimes. He served a jail sentence in the United States and has subsequently then been removed by our agency back to his home jurisdiction, Bosnia and Herzegovina, where he subsequently has pleaded guilty to his involvements in those crimes as he was charged by the Bosnian State War Crimes Court. So that particular case gives a good representation of the scope of the work of our unit, in general, and my work, in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, can you briefly describe what role you played in that? And we will, of course, get to your fundamental back -- you know, your education and your background, but just tell us where you fit into that -- to that investigation and/or prosecution.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: My role, specifically, and with our intelligence people, in general, is to provide the necessary background expertise to allow for our special agents to investigate the case properly, what areas that they should focus on. In my particular case, because of my detailed knowledge of Srebrenica, I obviously brought a good amount of information to the table in this particular case and, following that, worked with United States attorneys who are prosecuting the case in Boston. And ultimately in that case, I also testified as an expert witness as to the circumstances related to the Branjevo Farm massacres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you testified as an expert on Bosnia and former Yugoslav issues in the United States in other cases?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you testified as an expert in this Tribunal before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is my fifth occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the other cases were that you testified as an expert in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I testified initially in the case of the Prosecutor versus General Krstic. I testified as an expert in the case of the Prosecutor versus Blagojevic and Jokic. I testified in the case of Popovic et al. I testified in the case of the Prosecutor and -- versus Perisic. And so this is my fifth time in these courtrooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you testified as an expert in the State Court of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would like now to -- let's turn the page. It should be page 3 in English, where we go beyond your experience for the United States, and we start to talk about your experience in the United States Army. In fact, let's go to page 4. I want to work -- I want to work backwards and work up towards your job for the OTP. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it begins with the August 1981 through January 1989, various intelligence-related assignments as an enlisted soldier and, later, non-commissioned officer in the US Army. So can you tell us, did you enlist in the army at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I enlisted in August of 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And briefly describe, very briefly, those first eight years.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Briefly, those eight years were a mixture of intelligence postings at various military units, some of them strategic intelligence units, some of them tactical ground units, where I learned my profession at the very -- from the very bottom starting up, serving first as an enlisted soldier, then as a non-commissioned officer. That is -- that is the developmental, you know, plan, so that's where they sent me for the first eight years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how old were you when you first enlisted in the army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Goodness. Twenty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your grade or rank, if you could call it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I started as a private first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Like everyone else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Pretty much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And by the end of those eight years, until we get to the next segment on your CV, what was your rank or position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: When I finally left the non-commissioned officer corps and was appointed a warrant officer, I was a staff-sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, again briefly, what the difference is between a non-commissioned officer and a -- what you've just described as a warrant officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In the United States Army, the grades are broken down; enlisted soldiers, non-commissioned officers and officers. Officers -- at some juncture, all officers will hold a commission. In my particular field as a warrant officer, I'm not immediately commissioned. We are appointed to that position. And once being appointed for several years, I received my commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
