utterances.text: Let me interrupt. What's the difference between an appointment and a commission?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Functionally, there's no difference at all. It is just a holdover of the military tradition in one part, and in a second part it is a recognition that as I make that jump from the non-commissioned officer corps to the officer corps, it might not be permanent. If I fail to perform in the requisite manner, that appointment can be withdrawn and I would find myself reverted back to the non-commissioned officer corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We can't hear a thing, if Mr. Gajic is saying something.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps you can see that I'm on my feet for a long time after Mr. McCloskey and the witness are finishing speaking. The transcript is about six to seven lines ahead of the interpretation into B/C/S, so I would appreciate it if the witness and the Prosecutor would slow down a little, especially when using specialised terminology, because the interpreters find it sometimes hard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this information. We are not able to listen to the B/C/S translation, and, therefore, it is appreciated that you draw the attention to that fact. I realise that you, Mr. McCloskey, were talking quite slowly, but Mr. Butler should slow down a bit --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- and pause between question and answer. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We left off, I believe, where you had been a non-commissioned officer, as a sergeant, and you went into the ranks of the warrant officer. And can you explain, as a warrant officer, is that -- does that have the equivalent of any rank -- officer rank that we're used to hearing in every day parlance?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It does, and it is, in fact, a rank in -- recognised in the United States Army. Warrant officers are the technical experts of the army in various fields. We have different career paths from other officers, which is primarily designed to allow us to specialise in very narrow fields. So in that way, we're different from other officers who will take a more general career path and have a much broader range of experiences, many of them which will not even be related to the field that they specialise in, but will still require their officers experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So does it make any sense to compare you at all to a lieutenant, for example?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, it does not. I mean, in the grade of rank, the highest warrant officer is still not superior to the youngest lieutenant. However, in the function of position, a US Army second lieutenant will be an individual who is 22 or 23 years old, with very little actual experience and training, in the beginning of his developmental cycle in the army, where a warrant officer will be someone who already has 10, 15 or 20 years, perhaps even more for the senior warrant officers, in the developmental cycle in their specific field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We -- looking at your CV, we see that from February 1989 to 1992, you call yourself a Warrant -- you were a Warrant Officer 1, and later a Chief Warrant Officer 2, and your job description was that of an all-source evidence technician.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It should read "intelligence technician."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what an all-source intelligence technician -- what was your job?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: My job at that particular period was to analyse information that would come in from all aspects of either formal intelligence collection or other forms of information that, as a military unit, we would gain as part of our activities, traditional intelligence sources such as human intelligence, signals intelligence, imagery intelligence. It would -- non-traditional sources, such as the evaluation of open-source or publicly-available information that we would get from magazines or other military types of documents that were not necessarily classified but are part of a military's -- they produce them. So in that sense, it is all source. I was expected to be proficient in my ability to analyse and synthesise the information from all of those various disciplines of intelligence collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I know from the record and from -- as the Defence is aware, we are not allowed to get into -- nor is it particularly relevant to get into the specifics of your intel work in the field. But generally, were you doing this work of analysing this material ever in a combat zone, during armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you give us, roughly, the years that you would have been working in and around a combat zone in an armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In this particular context, it would be, I guess, what is now referred to as the first Gulf War. We called it Desert Storm back then. So that would be 1991, I believe, 1990-1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you in the field in the Gulf?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I was taken from the 3rd Infantry Division, and I was re-subordinated or attached, if you were, to the headquarters of United States 7th Corps which had already deployed to South-West Asia. So I joined the unit there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You've mentioned the kinds of materials that an all-source evidence technician analyses, but tell us for what purpose. What are you analyse -- just roughly, without specifics, what are you analysing, for what purpose, and who, if anyone, does your analysis or conclusions go to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The work that I did, specifically, given the context of the Gulf -- the first Gulf War, was to essentially analyse the combat dispositions and operations of the Iraqi Army for the purpose of targeting them and destroying their military capability during our offensive operations. As with any other military intelligence professional in our army, our ultimate customer is our commander, so the intelligence products that we worked on and that we produced were for the benefit of our commanders in order to make their precise plans and to, you know, as effectively and efficiently as possible, defeat the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you write reports for your command?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: My reports were both written and -- when time did not allow for them to be written, I gave verbal situation reports, not only to my command but, as required, to subordinate commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And during that wartime experience, can you describe the kinds of an all-source evidence that you were able to see and analyse, and was it similar to the material you've previously described?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Obviously, for a time the Iraqi military used radio communications, and there was intelligence derived from that. We had access to human intelligence, both in the form of civilians who would cross the lines and would provide us information as to where Iraqi military forces were dug in and in what strength, as well as once the actual conflict started, access to Iraqi prisoners of war, who would be debriefed, and we would then take their information and use it for our intelligence purposes. We obviously had access to imagery products, being that it was a desert, so we had an ability to use imagery in order to physically see the dispositions of the enemy forces. So in that context, that was the all-source analysis and production methodology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about documents, Iraqi military, political, or civilian documents; did you have access to any kind of material like that for your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Certainly after our offensive operations started and we began over-running Iraqi military positions and command posts, we had access to Iraqi military documents, operations orders, map graphics, which we would get immediately translated. And then using that information for our intelligence purposes, analyse it, process it, and get that information out to our corps commander, as well as the subordinate commands, so they had a more accurate picture of the enemy dispositions and what their military intentions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I think that will cover it for the US Army for me. We can refer to the CV for anything else. I now want to get to: How was it and when was it that you came to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I came to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY in April of 1997 as a, at that time, Chief Warrant Officer 3. The United States Government essentially seconded me to the ICTY Office of the Prosecutor in order to assist the Office of the Prosecutor in analysing military-related information in order to assist their investigators and their Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how long did you stay employed by the US Army? At some point, did you make a change?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: My initial assignment was scheduled to be two years. Because of circumstances related to the Srebrenica investigation, it lasted five. At that point, I had reached the 20-year mark of military service and was eligible for -- and I retired from active military service. At that point in time, the Office of the Prosecutor then hired me as a UN civil servant, I guess is the term of art, where I served from September 2001 to, essentially, November of 2003 as a UN employee, working the same job as I had before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, which case did you primarily work on during your time at the OTP?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The bulk of my professional work related to the Srebrenica-related cases that were under investigation and later trial by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Having in mind the description you just gave us of the kind of materials you analysed and reported on in combat for the United States Army, can you tell us, your work for the Srebrenica investigation and case, did it involve anything in terms of similar material or analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The work was remarkably similar to what I had done in the US Army. Initially, when I joined the investigation in probably around May/early June of 1997, most of the information related to what I would refer to as open-source information; magazine articles, newspaper articles, news videos that would depict aspects of the crime scene. Later, following searches by members of the Office of the Prosecutor of various military units, we gained access to military documents from various units of the Army of the Republika Srpska, particularly the Bratunac Brigade, the Zvornik Brigade, and some related to the Drina Corps. We then gained access to intercepted Bosnian Serb Army communications that were taken by the Bosnian Muslim military forces in and around July of 1995, so we actually had communications intelligence related to that. And, finally, I think we started, in 1997, getting access to interview military officers who were in official positions in July of 1995 related to Srebrenica, so we were able to interview them to have them fill in many of the blanks, to get their statements, so to speak. So in that context, much of the work that I did here for the Office of the Prosecutor is exactly what I did for the United States Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "military officers," primarily, were they from one side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: For the most part, these were military officers from the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your analysis work for the Office of the Prosecutor, did you get imagery products?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I am aware that the US Government, as part of their role in cooperating with the work of the Tribunal, had made available various overhead imagery products related to various aspects of the Srebrenica crime base, most of them pertaining to the locations of suspected mass graves, some of them actually showing photographs of groups of individuals who we later came to learn were captured prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, ever actively take part in the interview of officers of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was your function?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In a manner similar to what I do today, the first part of my job would be to work with the investigator who would be conducting the interview to bring that investigator fully up to speed with all the information that we had on an individual officer and what we believed his role might have been during the relevant period. The interviewer would then conduct, in most cases, the first part of the interview. At some point, if there were a particular military issue that needed to be explored or the answers that we were hearing were not answers that we had prepared for or had anticipated, the interviewer would ask me to step in and take over various parts of the interview in order to clarify issues or in order to deal with particularly technical issues of a military officer interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As part of your analysis of materials for the Office of the Prosecutor, did you review any laws related to armed conflict in the former Yugoslavia and any military regulations/rules that you believed or were possibly in effect at the time of the war in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I've reviewed a great deal of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you write any reports for the Office of the Prosecutor based on your analysis and review and involvement in the investigations and knowledge gained?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I've drafted a number of reports for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you go over just those reports briefly? And I mean, very briefly, because we all know that much of those reports are made up of the documents that we're going over. So if we could just -- so if you could first tell us what report you started off with, and what it was, and what its purpose was.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: My original two reports were the Srebrenica military narrative and the corps command responsibility report. In the particular context of the time, the accused was General Radislav Krstic, so the purpose of the corps command report was to examine the role of a corps commander within the Army of the Republika Srpska. And this report dealt with all of the structural, legal and military aspects of what it means to be a corps commander in a particular army, including what his duties and responsibilities were under the relevant law that the Army of the Republika Srpska was operating under, as well as the broader Law of War or International Humanitarian Law, which was also applicable to General Krstic at the time. The Srebrenica military narrative was designed to place the relevant military documents that were in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor in the context of the crime base and the military events that occurred related to Srebrenica. So the initial report was focused primarily from the period of 4 July to, roughly, 20 July 1995, and it essentially tells, in the form of a narrative, what various military documents and orders were issued at various times and how they relate to situations on the ground. And in that context of military documents, I also referred to the military intercepts from the BiH which also were integrated into that picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you cite and integrate into this narrative any statements of survivor witnesses or, as you've, I think, said, crime-base witnesses?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As a matter of practice here, I did not, or only did so to the absolute minimum degree required in order to set a particular crime so there would be some context. Unique to this situation in the legal aspect of this, as opposed to my own military one, you know, I am aware that many of these witnesses will obviously be testifying before the Tribunal and will give their own evidence, so I did not feel it was my place to incorporate their testimony from statements in any way into that, since that is, obviously, you know, more properly the role of the Court, not an analyst. So by design, wherever possible, I did not use statements from military officials that were interviewed. In the case of survivors, I only used it in order to set the context of a particular crime scene. For example, you have to have the statement of accounting of survivors from Orahovac to know when it happened and where in order to allow for the military documents and the communications intercepts to make any sense relating to that particular crime base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I see that it's break time, and this, I think, would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We must have our second break now, and we will resume in half an hour, quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you just briefly described your original narrative and your original command report on the corps for the Krstic case. Can you tell us, going as far back as Krstic, was the -- was there an issue in that case regarding the role of the corps commander and the role of the corps security officer, as well as the Main Staff security officer, their various roles and inter-relationships? Was that an issue in the Krstic case and in your command report and testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It was one of the primary themes of the Krstic defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just briefly tell us what you believed the theme of the Krstic defence was that you were -- that you were dealing with, not so much that that's an issue, but what were you dealing with, what was your perception of that defence that you had to deal with in your reports and your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The specific issues raised revolved around the assertions by General Krstic that, first of all, during the period he was not the corps commander and, secondly, that the Main Staff and security officers, exercising independent authorities, essentially hijacked the Drina Corps intelligence and security apparatus and the subordinate brigade security apparatus, and used them to commit the crimes, and as the commander, he had both -- or, actually, not even as the commander, but in the alternative, as the commander he had no knowledge, or no responsibility even if he had did have knowledge. So it was in that context where I laid out, as part of the corps command responsibility report, what his nominal role would have been as the commander, also as the chief of staff, during the various period, as well as the laws, rules and regulations of the military and how they pertained to both the functions of command as well as the functions of security within the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what sources were you able to look at to determine what a commander's responsibilities would have been in the VRS, or a security officer's responsibilities were? What did you look at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The initial sources, as they were obtained by the Office of the Prosecutor, were former operational regulations or manuals from the former Yugoslav national army. One of the working early theses that we had, as analysts, was that, to the largest degree possible, the Army of the Republika Srpska was following the rules, regulations and doctrines of the former Yugoslav national army that had then dissolved by then. Those rules, regulations and manuals lay out, in a good sense of detail, the roles and responsibilities of command as well as the roles and responsibilities of those involved in security and intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this Trial Chamber has seen, as part of this case, quite a few JNA, Peoples -- the army you referred to, JNA rules regarding command, security, and other key points. You said it was a working thesis. After your ability and the investigation's ability to interview VRS officers, have you reached a conclusion whether or not those JNA rules and regulations were actually used or not used by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, very early on in the interview process, we were able to confirm that information as we would interview these various officers, who told us that these were still in use, and further as we obtained military documents from the Army of the Republika Srpska, from the various searches that were done by the Office of the Prosecutor, not only myself but other military analysts from other cases, we could clearly see where, in some cases, entire passages from those former Yugoslav national army regulations were quoted in VRS documents as the procedures to be followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You have described your first two reports. Could you briefly tell us what other reports you had done?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The next series of reports were more directed towards issues coming up with the second Srebrenica-related trial, that of Colonel Blagojevic and that of Major Jokic. In that particular case, I was asked to do a command report, but to focus it on issues that were relevant to brigade command, since Colonel Blagojevic was the brigade commander of the Bratunac Brigade, as well as issues related to the duty officer roles at a brigade level and intelligence and security roles at the brigade level. So it was essentially taking the work from corps and dropping it down one echelon to the brigade level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And was there a revised narrative that you did as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In order to incorporate new information that had been learned as a result of the ongoing investigation from my previous narrative, I used that opportunity to incorporate that new material into what I call a revised narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I also see that you did something called a report, Chapter 8, Analytical Addendum to the Srebrenica-related Narrative, Revised. What was that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That particular chapter dealt with an issue that had cropped up relating to documents concerning individuals who were known to be in the custody of the Army of the Republika Srpska as either prisoners or wounded, and who later ended up disappeared. So that additional annex dealt primarily with individuals who were captured at the Milici -- or were known to have been captured by the VRS and were also known to have been treated at the Milici Medical Centre in July -- I believe it was July 12 or 13, who were subsequently transferred to Zvornik and then are now disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do these six reports comprise your full reporting on the events and the laws and the rules in play? Are there any others, is what I'm getting at.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The final report that I did was for the Popovic trial. Because of the issue of individuals who were members of the Main Staff who were on trial, I was asked by the Office of the Prosecutor to draft a report related to the roles and responsibilities of those various officers who were members of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I have 65 ter numbers for these six reports. And while they do have some overlap, as you may have gleaned from the description, they all deal with separate and new information, and I would like to -- I can provide a piece of paper with their numbers on it later, if that would save some time, or I can read them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They are only a few. It's, I think, the best way to put it on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let me start with Mr. Butler's updated CV, which is 65 ter 7436.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At this point in time, I would like to ask the Defence if there are any objections to add this document to the 65 ter exhibit list. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has no objection on this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, no. Wait a moment, please. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Then I would tender that 7436.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7436 shall be assigned Exhibit P2469. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the corps command report, 65 ter 651, and I would offer that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd just read out the numbers of the different reports you have dealt with, and then we will come to a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Those numbers are: 651, the command; 653 for the military narrative original; 652 for the brigade command; 654 for the revised narrative; 661 for the Chapter 8 analytical addendum; and 65 ter 2001 for the Main Staff report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it they are all on the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are there any objections by the Defence against their admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Registrar has drawn my attention to one problem. You are referring to 65 ter 661. That seems not to be included in the list of documents you have provided us with, but there is a document 662. Could you please check that again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, don't worry. It is found. That was a misinformation. I take it that there is no objection by the Defence against the admission of these documents. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Mr. President, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: These six documents will be received as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 651 shall be assigned Exhibit P2470. 65 ter document 653 shall be assigned Exhibit P2471. 65 ter document 652 shall be assigned Exhibit P2472. 65 ter document 654 shall be assigned Exhibit P2473. 65 ter document 661 shall be assigned Exhibit P2474. And, finally, 65 ter document 2001 shall be assigned Exhibit P2475. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, I also note that we have on the list a series of what we have referred to as proofing notes, which were lists of -- and packets of reports and materials that were provided you at various dates, and I see those are in 2007, 2008, two in 2008, and one in 2010. Can you just very briefly describe what you did when you were provided these packets of documents?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As the Court is aware, I've not been an employee of the Office of the Prosecutor since November of 2003. However, I am called back by the Office of the Prosecutor to testify in these various cases. In order to ensure that my reports and my analysis and understanding of the various issues remains current and is accurate, as part of that I asked to review new tranches of documents or materials that are related to the issues concerning my report and my prior analysis. So what normally happens is that, at various points in time, I will take a week or a ten-day period sometime prior to my testimony - sometimes it may be a month, sometimes it may be a year - to review new material that has come to light as a result of the ongoing investigation. As I review that material, I'm asked to comment on that, particularly with respect to does this new material change any of my previous analysis on any particular topic that I've discussed. My opinions as to what the material is and how it's relevant to any given situation is then incorporated by the Office of the Prosecutor into proofing notes and then made available to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us for this particular trial, the trial of General Tolimir, what have you done to prepare for your testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I believe it was late March or early April of 2010, I spent a week here reviewing new documents and materials related to General Tolimir, and, of course, some of them I had seen before, but not in the context of General Tolimir. Some of them were new documents that I've not seen at all. So, again, in that particular situation I reviewed the material, I commented on how it did or did not affect my previous analysis, and those were incorporated into notes. And then several weeks ago, when I came here to testify, there was a several-day period where additional new information was either provided to me or, in some cases, I wanted, myself, once I became aware of them, to review them because I thought they might have an impact on something that I had either said or on some previous analysis. So, again, I reviewed additional material and, I believe, a couple of witness statements as part of that last final proofing, and that information also, I believe, is incorporated into proofing notes and turned over to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to review any past testimonies?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I also reviewed individuals' testimony - I believe the specific case, the testimony of General Milovanovic as he testified here in the current trial - to determine, based obviously on his position within the Army of the Republika Srpska, whether or not my conclusions on the use of doctrine or other issues remains valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And aside from General Milovanovic's testimony in this case, did you review any other witnesses' testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe his name was - I'll probably butcher it, I'm sorry - Rakovic, but it was the intelligence and security officer for the Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, the Rogatica Brigade, who had been interviewed - and had testified here - by the Office of the Prosecutor. I was not previously aware of any information provided by him. And, again, given the context of what I talk about with the security organs, you know, I wanted to review his testimony in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does the name Razdoljac ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: There we go. Yes, sir, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall what his position was with the 1st Podrinje Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I believe he was the security officer, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe he was the logistics officer. I don't know if you --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I'm mistaken, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, I don't know, does the name Carkic ring any bells to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Not off-hand. It's some -- depending on when I reviewed the material, the name is not ringing the bell. I'm sure in you refreshed my memory, it will be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's all right. And aside from those two testimonies, have you followed this trial at all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And aside from some of the work that you've described related to the war in the former Yugoslavia that you did in your United States job, have you tried to keep up with the investigation and all the additional evidence and witnesses and things that have occurred over the many years since you haven't been here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Given my current job responsibilities with the Department of Homeland Security, and the fact that I deal now with global issues, unless I am dealing with a very specific Bosnian-related case, I just do not have the time or ability to continue to follow these cases as they proceed here in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, fair enough. Now -- Mr. President, it's my plan now to change gears a little bit. So if there's any questions regarding Mr. Butler's background or expertise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Gajic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can see that things are speeding up. Until a moment ago, the speakers were following a tempo that the interpreters can follow. I would just like to draw everyone's attention to this problem, not only because of the transcript, but it happened at the end of the last session. The guard was urging Mr. Tolimir to stand up because he was still busy listening to the interpretation that was late. We have to deal with this problem also with the Guards Service. Of course, Mr. Tolimir and I want to do nothing that would be disrespectful of this Trial Chamber, but I really need to draw everyone's attention to this issue because sometimes even at the end of the day, when the session is over, the interpretation is still going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I saw and I heard you speaking very fast -- very much faster than Mr. McCloskey, and we had to wait for the interpretation. It is an ongoing problem, of course, in this and all other trials, and everybody is invited to do his best to let the interpreters translate everything which is said in the courtroom. Mr. McCloskey, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. McCloskey said he was moving on to a new area, and said that it was a good opportunity to ask general questions on the witness's background and experience. Mr. Witness, what difference do you make between your work as an intelligence officer and the work of a police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The work of an intelligence officer is geared primarily towards the collection of and the analysing of information in a military context related to a potential adversarial armed force, politically to an opposing government. From a law enforcement or police context, it is related to law enforcement. The fundamental methodologies of the collection and the processing and analysis of the information is the same. Where you have a difference is with respect to what I would call the output. From an intelligence perspective, my goal would be to take that information and, in a predictive nature, to advise my superior what future events may transpire, and give my superior the ability to affect those future effects. From a law enforcement perspective, a police perspective, that intelligence is used to define a static event or situation that has already occurred in the past and to gather as much information and to clarify it, as possible, so the crime can be properly investigated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. According to you, an immigration and customs officer can also -- can be an intelligence officer as well as a judicial police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. In my particular agency, as an intelligence officer, my role is to provide criminal intelligence support and analysis. While, as an immigration officer, I have some limited functions with respect to law enforcement, in our particular agency the majority of the law enforcement activities are undertaken by what we call special agents. Those are individuals who are specifically trained for and certified to conduct domestic law enforcement investigations in the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How about customs; is it the same? Because there is immigration and customs enforcement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It is a reflection of the fact that after the events that occurred in 9/11 and the Department of Homeland Security was created in 2003, the Immigration Agency and the Customs Agency were joined together as one singular law enforcement agency. So as a result, the particular agency has all of the enforcement powers of immigration, as well as all of the enforcement powers of customs enforcement, as well as retaining other criminal and civil investigative authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I understand better now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one additional question. Is this particular institution more an executive institution or an administrative institution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A combination of both, sir. In the United States, the investigative portion, we are -- ICE is an investigative agency. The application of immigration law in the United States is an application of -- it's considered administrative law. So in that sense, where individuals are placed in removal proceedings, while they are judicial, they are administrative, they are not criminal. We also have, of course, our abilities to investigate crimes related to both immigration and custom and other activities, but in that sense, where we take cases to court criminally, just like, for example, the FBI, we are not the investigator and the prosecutor. Those cases are brought by the United States Attorney's Office or the Department of Justice. So we do have both criminal and civil authorities or administrative authorities in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I recall that Mr. Gajic has helpfully noted that in the Serbian, they heard, in your discussion of aerial imagery, the term "unmanned aerial imagery." Did you ever say or suggest whether this aerial imagery was manned or unmanned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I don't recall that I did, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to clarify that for the record. Now, I would now begin to just go into some of the documents that get us started in the former Yugoslavia, and I would go past, in our books, tab 2, which is your old CV, to tab 3 and ask that we put up I believe it's 65 ter 1976. And this is a document that is dated 12 of May, 1992, entitled "Information About Post Assignments Delivered." And it's to the commander, personally. And we see at the bottom: "Command of the 5th Corps." Now, can you tell us: What army is this a document from, going back to this date of 12 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: At this time, we're discussing the Yugoslav national army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can just see from this document references to decrees, assigning General Mladic to the post -- well, two different posts - I won't read them - 1 and 2, and then, by the same decree [Realtime transcript read in error "degree"], it talks about, as we can see before us, jobs for Milan Gvero, Djordje Djukic, and Colonel Zdravko Tolimir. Can you just put this in context for us? May 12th, this is the JNA. What is this document doing? How does it relate, if at all, to the creation of -- and the formation of the VRS, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The particular document discusses personnel assignments to the Staff and Command of the 2nd Military District, which was at that time the over-arching JNA command dealing with Bosnia and Herzegovina. The 5th Corps was one of their subordinate corps, which would later become known as the 1st Krajina Corps when the JNA withdrew and it was redesignated. Many of the officers who were assigned to the 2nd Military District, particularly if they were of Bosnian Serb ethnicity, when the JNA pulled out of Bosnia and Herzegovina, those officers later formed the nucleus of what would be then known as the VRS Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, on page 74, line 4, would you agree that the word "degree" should read as "decree"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it should be, as we see from the document, "decree," d-e-c-r-e-e.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1976 shall be assigned Exhibit P2476. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, can we go to tab 4. It's P22.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a document, as we wait for it to come up, entitled "Decision on Strategic Objectives of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And we see down the left-hand corner a date, both languages, of 12 May 1992. Now, the Court has seen this before, and I don't want to get into it in a lot of detail, but do you recall, Mr. Butler, we see that this -- well, can you just tell us what this is a section taken out of? What is this decision? And we see it's in the name of Momcilo Krajisnik. Just very briefly, what is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not the document, so much, I'm sorry, but the -- where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As part of the Bosnian Serb Assembly session where they essentially begin the creation of their own state and their own army, a series of strategic objectives are laid out as part of the discussions. For whatever reason, while these strategic objectives are laid out in that Assembly meeting, it was not until 1993, I believe mid-1993, when the information was actually published in the Official Gazette, laying these out as formal strategic objectives. So these objectives that you see here are part of the discussions laid out in context at that 12 May Assembly meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, unfortunately, it didn't make it on the translation, but if we look at the Cyrillic up in the left-hand corner, we see the date of 1993. Actually, the 26th of a month of 1993. Is that what you're referring to when you say "a date in 1993"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, and I see it's 7.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that this should be "November 1993."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I hear no objection to that, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Defence, indeed --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have to adjourn for the day. Sir, as you know, there is no permission to have contact about the content of your testimony with either party during the break. We adjourn now and resume tomorrow, in the morning, at 9.00 in Courtroom III, in this courtroom. And we wait a moment until the translation has finished. We adjourn.
